explanation: Being allowed to inspect information does not necessarily mean that information must appear on every page. In the reviewed case, an administrator could obtain account information through administration pages, but another person's public profile deliberately hid it. A report matches when it treats that omission from the public page as loss of the administrator's access without checking the supported administration route. A failure to retrieve the information through the authorized route would be a different claim.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, follow this workflow: As a regular user, enable Hide Email Address in Settings. Open your own profile and hover the padlock next to your email. As an administrator, open that user's profile and look for the email. The rejected report expected: The reported expectation is that an administrator sees the hidden email on the user's profile page, as the tooltip suggests. It claimed this outcome: With Hide Email Address on, the user's own profile showed the email with a padlock reading 'Your email address is only visible to you and administrators'; an administrator opening the same profile saw no email row. Review concluded: Intended, and the message is accurate: administrators can see a hidden email, in Site Administration > User Accounts (the user list has an Email column) and on the admin Edit User page. The tooltip doesn't promise the profile page, where a hidden email is deliberately shown to no one else, administrators included (go-gitea/gitea#23900 added the padlock to say the email isn't visible to anyone apart from the user and the admins).

explanation: A browser can restore a page it displayed earlier when the user presses Back, without receiving that content again from the server. This pattern matches a security report based on seeing previously public content in that restored page after access was restricted, while fresh requests are correctly denied. Distinguish the browser's retained copy from a new unauthorized response. If a fresh request still returns protected content, that is a separate access-control claim.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, follow this workflow: As an observer, visit another user's profile and its Public Activity tab. As that user, set User visibility to Private in profile settings and save. As the observer, reload the activity tab, then use the browser's Back button to return to an earlier profile page. Check whether the server returns the profile or a 404. The rejected report expected: The reported expectation is that the private profile's ?tab=activity URL returns 404, like the base profile URL. It claimed this outcome: After the profile was made private, every fresh load of the profile and of its ?tab=activity URL by an unrelated user returned 404, including direct navigation, reloads and new tabs. The old public page reappeared only on the browser's Back button, served from the browser's own cache; reloading that page returned 404. The base profile behaves the same way on Back. Review concluded: Not a Gitea leak: the server checks visibility before rendering any profile tab, so the activity tab returns 404 to unrelated users once the profile is private. The only way to see the old page was the browser restoring a cached copy loaded while the profile was still public; Gitea deliberately sends private, must-revalidate caching rather than no-store so Back and history work. The report's own notes say the disclosure didn't recur and that the same history entry later returned 404.

explanation: A permission test must use an account that is actually subject to the restriction being tested. This pattern matches a report claiming that a protected operation can be bypassed after an administrator performs it, when the product expressly exempts administrators from that restriction. The administrator's success does not show that an ordinary restricted account can do the same thing. Verify the actor's effective role and repeat with a genuinely restricted user before alleging an access-control failure.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, follow this workflow: As one user, block a site administrator account. As the administrator, open the blocking user's profile and click Follow. Refresh and check whether the follow was accepted. The rejected report expected: The reported expectation is that a blocked user can't follow the user who blocked them. It claimed this outcome: The blocked account was a site administrator; its Follow succeeded and persisted after a refresh. Non-administrator blocked users are prevented from following. Review concluded: Intended: blocks don't apply to site administrators. Gitea deliberately treats an administrator as not blocked (its blocking documentation says a blocked user with admin permissions can still perform all actions), and blocks against regular users are enforced.

explanation: After browser Back, a search box can retain text that is not the query applied to the restored page. That text may even have been submitted at a later point in history; in the reviewed cases the address and results correctly returned to the earlier search. This pattern matches a report that treats the box text alone as proof that the active query or results are wrong. Verify the restored submitted query and results separately; a later action silently applying the retained text or returning incorrect results is outside this rejection.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, follow this workflow: On a user profile Repositories tab, search for a uniquely named repository A and confirm its matching result. Search for a different uniquely named repository B and confirm its matching result. Press browser Back and compare the URL, visible query field and results. Observe A in the URL and results while B remains in the search field. The rejected report expected: The report expects the visible search text to restore A together with its results. It claimed this outcome: The browser restores the last typed field value B, while the response input value attribute, URL and repository results correctly restore A. Normal submissions, Forward and navigation without editing the field are consistent. Review concluded: User rejected the reported draft-only display mismatch, consistent with gitea-pass2-007. Both reviewers reproduced the mismatch but disagreed on classification: Claude rejected it as browser-restored draft state, while Codex recommended acceptance at severity 1. This rejection is the explicit human judgment; it does not claim the observation failed to reproduce. A later Sort action applying the visible draft was observed separately and is excluded from this rejection, as are hidden filters or incorrect server search results.

explanation: A report's specific factual claim is contradicted by a decisive observation or by a controlled repetition of the same setup. For example, the allegedly deleted value is still present, or the allegedly broken control performs the requested action when activated as described. Match this pattern only when that counterevidence addresses the same value, action and conditions; a vaguely similar successful workflow is insufficient. The finding rejects the checked allegation, not every related defect or every possible historical failure.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, follow this workflow: Open user Settings > Profile. Remove the Location input's maxlength attribute and enter 51 characters. Click Update Profile and reload. The rejected report expected: The reported expectation is a validation error and no save. It claimed this outcome: The report described 'Your profile has been updated.' and a stored Location of the first 50 characters after removing the input's maxlength and submitting 51 characters. Review concluded: Not reproducible, and the server can't do it: UpdateProfileForm.Location is bound with MaxSize(50) (services/forms/user_form.go) and routers/web/user/setting/profile.go returns on ctx.HasError() before UpdateUser, so 51 or more characters (form, programmatic value, direct POST, CJK) shows 'form.Location must contain at most 50 characters.' and nothing is saved. The only success-plus-50-characters path is the browser's own maxlength=50 on the input (templates/user/settings/profile.tmpl) cutting the typed text before submit, so the server never receives 51. The validation re-render discarding the other unsaved fields is the separate accepted entry 'Profile edits are cleared after invalid Website URL submission'.

In Gitea, follow this workflow: Open Settings > Appearance at desktop or mobile width. Use the normal theme dropdown to select a theme and compare its visible label with the selection saved by Update Theme. The original claim requires a second visible native select; verify whether one is actually available without modifying the DOM. The rejected report expected: The reported expectation is one visible theme selection matching the value that Update Theme saves. It claimed this outcome: The report describes a visible native select and stale dropdown label. The supplied verification instead shows one visible dropdown with synchronized label and submitted value during normal mouse/keyboard selection; the native select is hidden. Review concluded: User rejected the original report as not reproduced through the rendered UI. The pinned dropdown stylesheet hides its native select with display:none!important, and the supplied verification shows normal selections updating the visible label and submitted value together. This rejection does not cover the separately discovered browser Back variant that restores a hidden form value without updating its label; that variant was not graded or credited to this report.

explanation: A report can judge the current application using a rule that applied to an older version. Reviewed Gitea examples are assuming admin remains a reserved username after administration moved to /-/admin, and demanding a five-second profiling minimum after the supported minimum became one second. Match this mistake only when the rejection record establishes the relevant intentional version change and the observed behavior follows the current rule. A failure of the current rule or a distinct missing-feedback defect remains separate; do not reject a report merely because a feature changed historically.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, follow this workflow: As a non-admin test user, open Settings > Profile. Change Username to admin and click Update Profile. Open /admin. The rejected report expected: The reported expectation is an error that 'admin' is reserved, with the username unchanged. It claimed this outcome: The rename succeeded with 'Your profile has been updated.', and /admin showed the user's profile. Review concluded: Intended in this version (1.24). 'admin' was reserved only while Site Administration lived at /admin. go-gitea/gitea#32189 (shipped in 1.23) moved the admin routes to /-/admin and removed "admin" from reservedUsernames in models/user/user.go, resolving go-gitea/gitea#32181, which asked to allow a user named admin (SSO setups using that name failed with 'name is reserved'). The pinned list holds only top-level paths still in use (api, user, explore, org, repo, issues, ...), which is why explore and user are rejected. With a user named admin, /-/admin stays reachable and the navbar links there; /admin showing that user's profile is normal /{username} routing.

explanation: This benchmark is a curated evaluation with rules about which kinds of findings count. A report matches this pattern when its only established issue falls outside those rules, such as an accessibility-tree-only label problem with no accepted visible or pointer-driven failure, an invalid state reachable only through an API, or an expressly excluded exotic input. The mistake is assuming that every technical imperfection is eligible for this evaluation. Scope exclusion does not establish that the underlying issue is imaginary, and a separately demonstrated in-scope functional failure must be assessed independently.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, follow this workflow: Sign in and open /user/settings; inspect the User visibility dropdown. Open /user/settings/appearance; inspect the Theme and Language dropdowns. The rejected report expected: The reported expectation is that each control's accessible name matches its visible label. It claimed this outcome: The Fomantic dropdowns have no aria-label or aria-labelledby and their visible labels are not associated; selecting values with the mouse works. Review concluded: Out of scope: this is screen-reader accessibility (label association on visually labelled controls), not a functional defect. The dropdowns open, select and save normally with the mouse. Accessibility findings are excluded from this benchmark's ground truth.

In Gitea, follow this workflow: Sign in, open another user's profile and click Block user. Press Shift+Tab from the focused note field. The rejected report expected: The reported expectation is that focus stays inside the modal and the modal is exposed as a named dialog. It claimed this outcome: Shift+Tab from the note field focused the footer API link while the modal stayed open; the modal has neither role=dialog nor aria-modal. Review concluded: Out of scope: this is keyboard-only accessibility (focus trapping and dialog semantics), not a functional defect. The behaviour is as described (templates/shared/user/block_user_dialog.tmpl and blocked_users.tmpl use a plain Fomantic modal, whose a11y gaps Gitea documents in web_src/js/modules/fomantic/aria.md), but the modals' Cancel, Block and Save buttons work with the mouse. Keyboard and accessibility findings are excluded from this benchmark's ground truth.
